rv.q: This is theatre to make the heart leap: a blazing beacon to progress, to possibility, to freedom and the power of imagination.
This adaptation doesn't attempt to be as radical in our time as Woolf was in hers, but it's still splendid in every sense: passionate, camp as Christmas and as warmly celebratory, too.
Like its star, Neil Bartlett’s giddy adaptation of Virginia Woolf’s novel radiates gleeful intelligence, rampaging heart and tremendous fun.

A captivating Corrin – a timeless, ageless pixie with a shock of white hair – inhabits the role to perfection, combining the dash and dazzle of a kingfisher with the casual sense of entitlement of an aristo.
True to Woolf’s spirit, the show’s strongest charm really is its inventiveness and creativity, and its final scene, though a little polemical, is a triumph, finding a conduit to genuine emotion.
What anchors attention is the coruscating Corrin.
A larky, optimistic evening fully exploiting Corrin's magnetism but one that's Rizla-thin.

It’s tricksy stuff, but Corrin largely anchors it, deftly fluctuating between masculine and feminine, always riveting to watch, even though Orlando is more an expression of an idea than a fully-fledged character.
If it is underpowered intellectually, that may be the price one pays for the absence of polemic.
There are lots of good things about this ‘Orlando’, but it’s just too brief, to not enough end.
Performances and design of unique warmth and wit create an outstandingly original theatrical pleasure.
Throughout, this is a fantastic performance, full of gentle detail – shoulders wriggling in distaste, eyes wide in discovery – and Corrin provides the compelling heart of a problematic play.
This is a giddy and enthralling production of a unique story that feels like a breath of fresh air.
Corrin’s gorgeous performance lifts the 90 minutes, no intermission, well beyond anything resembling a history lesson or a night out requiring preparatory homework.
This compact version, presenting its serious themes lightly, has a freshness that is very entertaining.

The Bartlett/Grandage collaboration weaves plenty of interesting strands, and the threads wander in different directions before eventually tying up loose ends in the twenty-first century with a rare moment of clarity for Orlando.

Emma Corrin is fortunately a charismatic stage presence, suggesting the slightly swaggering masculinity of the young Orlando and the confident female sexuality of the elder, connecting the two together in one consistent character with Corrin as watchable as ever.
But don’t expect a thunderclap.

Their performance is a glorious feat of shapeshifting, from wide-eyed boy to swaggering, sexy nobleman and self-possessed lady – while always retaining the soul of the character, their curious mind, quick wit and passionate heart.

Though economical, Bartlett’s adaptation is ultimately an incomplete and unfulfilling reworking of a novel that could have easily provided this cast and production team with at least another 90 minutes’ worth of material.
Although it looks sensational, it’s an eccentric triviality aimed at 1970s feminists.
It is absolutely wonderful and as much a love letter to theatre as a joyful interrogation of sex, gender and love.
The show becomes an optimistic celebration.
Emma Corrin is completely captivating in this transgender role with a wide eyed innocence that convinces Orlando’s lack of aging and magnetic charm over the centuries.
Emma Corrin stuns in poetically crafted gender play.
There’s a certain wittiness to the script that gives the audience a few chuckles, but it’s not enough to keep anyone fully engaged.
Overall it is an enjoyable watch and very well done.
Corrin certainly takes us on a fun ride along the way.

cn.t: Critics praise Emma Corrin's captivating performance and Neil Bartlett's inventive adaptation, calling the production joyful and timely. Most laud Michael Grandage's direction for its lightness of touch, though some find it overly contemporary or missing the mark.
